lesson.title: Where younger readers find the news

learning_objectives.en: Locate details in a multi-paragraph report, recognise paraphrases and match information to paragraphs.
learning_objectives.vi: Tìm thông tin trong bài nhiều đoạn, nhận diện cách diễn đạt lại và ghép thông tin với đoạn.

content.en: Read each statement first; underline the information type (number, comparison, example, explanation). Skim paragraphs for their function and scan only the candidate paragraphs. A paragraph can answer more than once; questions may not follow passage order.
content.vi: Đọc yêu cầu và gạch từ khóa về loại thông tin (số liệu, so sánh, ví dụ, giải thích). Đọc lướt để tìm chức năng đoạn rồi quét dòng bằng chứng. Một đoạn có thể trả lời nhiều câu; không mặc định cùng thứ tự.

example.en: a surprising claim -> check another source
example.vi: thông tin gây ngạc nhiên -> kiểm tra ở nguồn thứ hai

content.en: An option can repeat a word from the passage but express the opposite meaning. Decide from the meaning of a complete sentence.
content.vi: Phương án có thể lặp từ nguyên văn nhưng trái nghĩa. Dựa vào nghĩa cả câu.

example.en: rarely visit deliberately ≠ never read news
example.vi: hiếm khi chủ động truy cập ≠ không bao giờ xem tin

vocabulary.example_en: Media literacy involves verifying dates and authors.
vocabulary.example_vi: Hiểu biết truyền thông đòi hỏi kiểm tra ngày tháng và tác giả.

vocabulary.example_vi: Việc tình cờ tiếp xúc có thể giúp người đọc biết chủ đề mới.

strategies.en: 1 Identify information type; 2 skim all paragraphs; 3 scan candidates for synonyms; 4 confirm a full-sentence match.
strategies.vi: 1 Xác định loại thông tin; 2 lướt toàn bài; 3 dò từ đồng nghĩa; 4 kiểm tra cả câu.

common_mistakes.wrong: Young people are not interested in news.
common_mistakes.correct: Young people often encounter news incidentally.

reason.en: The passage challenges a broad generalisation.
reason.vi: Bài đọc bác bỏ sự khái quát quá mức và nêu cách tiếp cận tin tức mang tính tình cờ.

passages.title: How younger audiences find the news
passages.text:
[A] Ask a group of eighteen-year-olds where they last read a news story and very few will mention a newspaper. Most will name an app, a video platform or a message forwarded by a friend. This shift has worried many journalists, who fear that young people are no longer interested in the news. A three-year study of 1,200 people aged sixteen to twenty-four in the fictional country of Valdor suggests a more complicated picture: young people do follow the news, but they meet it in different ways and judge it by different standards.

[B] The most common route to the news, the study found, is accidental. Rather than deciding to read about current events, young people usually come across a story while doing something else – scrolling through photos, watching a comedy clip or chatting with friends. Around seventy per cent of participants said that most of the news they saw in a typical week had appeared in this way. Only one in five regularly visited a news website or app on purpose.

[C] This accidental exposure has advantages. It brings news to people who might never look for it, including those who say they find politics boring. However, the researchers noted that stories reached participants through systems designed to keep them watching, not to inform them. A dramatic video about a minor event could be seen by millions, while an important but less exciting decision by the government might not appear at all. Several participants admitted that they knew a great deal about celebrity disputes but very little about changes to student loans.

[D] Trust was another major theme. Participants did not trust news organisations simply because they were large or well known. Instead, they paid attention to who had shared a story and whether it seemed to be supported by evidence such as videos, documents or interviews. Many said they trusted an ordinary person filming an event more than a news presenter describing it. The researchers pointed out that this attitude can be healthy, since it encourages people to look for proof, but it also makes young audiences vulnerable to edited or misleading clips.

[E] When participants did want to understand a story properly, their habits changed. Asked what they did after seeing a surprising claim, nearly half said they searched for the same story on another source to check it. Short explainer videos and podcasts were especially popular for complicated topics such as the economy or climate policy. One participant described podcasts as “the only place where someone explains the whole story, not just the angry part”.

[F] Local news presented a particular challenge. Few participants could name a local newspaper or radio station, and many were unaware of decisions made by their town council. Yet when the researchers showed them stories about local issues – a closed youth centre, a new bus route, a plan to build flats on a sports field – interest was high. The problem, the researchers concluded, was not a lack of interest but a lack of contact: local stories rarely appear on the platforms that young people use most.

[G] Some news organisations have responded by changing how they work. In Valdor, a regional newspaper now employs two reporters who produce short videos about local stories specifically for social media, and a public broadcaster has started a weekly programme presented by people under twenty-five. Early figures suggest that these efforts reach far more young people than the organisations’ websites, although it is not yet clear whether viewers go on to read longer reports.

[H] The study’s authors argue that schools also have a role to play. Teaching students how stories are selected, how images can be edited and how to compare sources could help them make better use of the news they meet by accident. In their view, the aim should not be to persuade young people to return to traditional newspapers, but to help them become careful, questioning readers wherever they find the news.

instruction.en: Read the complete passage. Write A–H for the paragraph containing the information. A letter may be used twice.

questions.prompt_en: A numerical estimate for news encountered unintentionally.
questions.prompt_vi: Số liệu về tin vô tình gặp.

questions.prompt_en: One danger of using systems built to retain attention.
questions.prompt_vi: Một nguy cơ của thuật toán giữ chân người dùng.
questions.explanation_en: Algorithms can favour drama over public importance.
questions.explanation_vi: Hệ thống có thể ưu tiên yếu tố giật gân hơn tầm quan trọng xã hội.
questions.evidence: [C] systems designed to keep them watching

questions.prompt_en: Why large and established publishers are not automatically trusted.
questions.prompt_vi: Vì sao tổ chức báo lớn không được mặc định tin tưởng.
questions.explanation_en: Trust is based on evidence and who shared the report, not only size.
questions.explanation_vi: Độ tin dựa trên bằng chứng và người chia sẻ, không chỉ quy mô.
questions.evidence: [D] did not trust news organisations simply because

questions.prompt_en: The participant age range and sample size.
questions.prompt_vi: Độ tuổi và cỡ mẫu khảo sát.
questions.explanation_vi: Đoạn mở đầu nêu 1.200 người 16–24 tuổi.

questions.prompt_en: What some readers do when they need a deeper explanation.
questions.prompt_vi: Việc người đọc làm khi muốn hiểu sâu.
questions.explanation_en: They seek a second source or explanations.
questions.explanation_vi: Họ tìm nguồn khác và thông tin giải thích.

questions.prompt_en: An example of a dramatic but relatively unimportant story.
questions.prompt_vi: Ví dụ tin gây sốc nhưng ít quan trọng.
questions.explanation_en: The passage contrasts a viral minor event with a government decision.
questions.explanation_vi: Bài so sánh sự kiện nhỏ nhưng lan truyền mạnh với quyết định chính phủ.

questions.prompt_en: A reason to welcome and question ordinary eyewitness videos.
questions.prompt_vi: Lý do vừa đánh giá cao vừa thận trọng với video nhân chứng.
questions.explanation_en: Looking for evidence can help, but clips may be edited.
questions.explanation_vi: Tìm bằng chứng có lợi nhưng clip có thể bị chỉnh sửa.

questions.prompt_en: The difference between being exposed to news and deliberately searching for it.
questions.prompt_vi: Khác biệt giữa gặp tin và chủ động tìm kiếm.
questions.explanation_en: Seventy per cent encounter it unintentionally, only one in five actively visit a news site.
questions.explanation_vi: 70% gặp tin tình cờ; chỉ một phần năm thường chủ động truy cập trang tin.

instruction.en: Answer with ONE TO THREE WORDS OR A NUMBER from the passage.
instruction.vi: Trả lời 1–3 từ hoặc một con số lấy từ bài.
